LEADERSHIP & TRANSFORMATION / 03

Transformation starts
with strong ground.

AI-enabled delivery changes the work, the responsibilities and the habits around software. Give people a clear purpose and practical ways to make that change their own.

Shervin Sadeghi · Scope AI · 2 November 2026

IN THIS ARTICLE

Understand the workEstablish strong groundMake change workableCreate meaning and ownershipLearn through a real incrementTwo ways to helpPerspective and attribution

A team can adopt a coding assistant and still struggle to deliver. Requirements remain unclear. Review queues grow. People are uncertain about what they now own. Scope AI approaches AI-enabled software delivery as a change in how a team works together.

Start with the people doing the work.

Before choosing tools, understand the current reality. Where does work wait? What repeatedly comes back for clarification? Which practices already protect quality? Ask analysts, developers, testers and release owners about the pressures they face and what they hope to gain.

A developer's concern about generated code may reveal a real review burden. A tester's hesitation may expose unclear acceptance criteria. Treat these observations as design inputs. The team’s capacity to learn and review is part of the delivery problem.

Agree what the change must protect.

For Scope AI, strong ground means clear purpose, understood commitments and honest engagement with reality. Agree the outcome, the quality expectations, the scope and who owns consequential decisions. Be explicit about what is known and what needs testing.

For a delivery pilot, the objective might be to reduce requirement-related rework while preserving business correctness. Agree how that will be measured before introducing a new workflow. Avoid promising savings before understanding the current effort.

Build the practical support.

Our use of “plumbing” describes the processes, tools, responsibilities and support that make change workable. In software delivery, this includes a shared domain language, focused specifications, manageable tasks, appropriate design patterns, behavioural tests and reviewed pull requests.

It also includes learning time, access to experienced reviewers and a clear route for uncertainty. Decide what an agent may do, which decisions require people, and what happens when a requirement or test result is unclear. Existing delivery gates connect those decisions to evidence.

ILLUSTRATIVE DELIVERY SITUATION

An assistant generates changes faster, but the reviewer now receives large diffs with unexplained assumptions. The team tries smaller end-to-end tasks, explicit business rules and requirement-linked tests. The pilot measures total delivery and review effort to see whether the change helps.

The tools support this method. They are selected and adapted for the team’s needs rather than treated as a complete transformation in themselves.

Help people find meaning and ownership.

“Poetry” is our shorthand for connecting change to people's experience and contribution. Explain how the proposed practices address the burdens they described. Invite the team to shape the workflow and make clear how its feedback changes the design.

An analyst may spend more time resolving business ambiguity. A developer may focus more on design decisions and reviewing generated changes. A tester may help challenge assumptions earlier. These are possibilities to explore with people, not fixed roles to impose.

Discuss tensions honestly. More output may mean more review work. Learning requires time. Empathy and clear expectations belong together: people need both a voice in the change and an understanding of their commitments.

Learn through a real increment.

Choose a pilot small enough to inspect and meaningful enough to test the benefit. Establish a baseline, a method version, review timing and conditions to continue, adjust or stop.

Measure time to accepted software, total effort including specification and review, rework, defects and cost. Ask who benefited, who absorbed extra work, and whether the team can maintain the process. A passing deployment alone does not answer those questions.

Scope AI is developing its own delivery method in the same way. Each iteration should deliver working software and evidence about the method. Useful lessons become reusable guidance; practices that add burden without value should change. Internal learning informs client pilots without assuming that every environment is the same.

Two services, a shared leadership foundation.

Agentic Workflow Design & Delivery helps a client improve a business process using agents, integrations and defined human authority.

AI-Enabled Software Delivery Transformation helps a client’s team change how it builds and maintains software. The engagement combines assessment, an adapted method, a measured pilot, coaching and handover.

A client can choose either service independently. Both begin with people, purpose and accountable decisions. The transformation should leave the team able to own and sustain the improvement.

START WITH ONE DELIVERY CHALLENGE

What would better delivery mean for your team?

Bring a recurring bottleneck, a review burden or an unclear handoff. We can start by understanding the work and defining a useful pilot.

Perspective and attribution

This article presents Scope AI’s leadership philosophy and proposed approach to delivery transformation. The founder’s reading of Brené Brown’s Strong Ground, including the ideas of strong ground and plumbing and poetry, inspired this direction. The definitions and applications here are Scope AI’s interpretations, not quotations, an authoritative summary of the book or a claim of endorsement.

The delivery situation is illustrative. No client results or quantified improvements are claimed; the method requires validation through real work.
